text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Chancellor Kohl says existing pay contracts must be respected, despite cut in statutory sick pay
- Construction industry association says minimum wage should be kept in force until May 1997 at most
- IfW institute says economic recovery continuing
- President of Federal Labour Office cautions against expecting tougher unemployment benefit rules to get many off dole queue
HANDELSBLATT
- Chancellor Kohl says existing pay contracts must be respected, despite cut in statutory sick pay
- Opposition Social Democrat leader Lafontaine makes clear his party will not approve scrapping of wealth tax
- Finance Minister Waigel says market gaining confidence in new European currency
- Municipal revenue rises
- German import prices fall in August
- Presidium of industry federation BDI proposes re-election of Hans-Olaf Henkel as president
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- President Roman Herzog says he will not stay for second term of office beyond 1999
- Calls grow for closer checks on early release of sex criminals after killing of seven-year-old girl
- Chancellor Kohl says existing pay contracts must be respected
- Presidium of industry federation BDI proposes re-election of Hans-Olaf Henkel as president
- Row escalates in EU over how to finance agricultural payments
- Import and export prices fall in August
- Bundesbank president Tietmeyer says there is no way back once EU single currency is introduced
- Communes' deficits cut by half in first half of 1996
DIE WELT
- Chancellor Kohl says existing pay contracts must be respected, despite cut in statutory sick pay
- Brandenburg premier Stolpe says new accusations of cooperation with East German secret police are delibetrae slander
- Presidium of industry federation BDI unanimously proposes re-election of Hans-Olaf Henkel as president
- Communes' finances improve in first half of 1996
- Finance Minister Waigel says market gaining confidence in new European currency
- More and more self-employed rebel against membership of chambers of commerce
